evidence.claim: Granite mountains, lakes and shoreline linked by an island motor road
evidence.quote: This 27-mile (43 km) road is the go-to scenic drive around the east side of Mount Desert Island, connecting Acadia's lakes, mountains, and shoreline.

evidence.claim: Granite mountains
evidence.quote: From craggy shorelines and granite-capped mountains to crystal lakes and spruce–fir forests

evidence.claim: The Acadia All-American Road runs from Trenton through Bar Harbor and onto the Park Loop Road, linking the mainland approach with Mount Desert Island’s eastern landscape.
evidence.quote: From Trenton, Maine, following Route 3, this byway follows Route 3 into Bar Harbor, then follows the park loop road thereafter.

evidence.claim: Mount Desert Island’s eastern landscape
evidence.quote: around the east side of Mount Desert Island

evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration lists a 40-mile All-American Road and recommends three hours to drive and see it.
evidence.quote: All-American Road • Maine Length 40 mi / 64.4 km Time to Allow Take three hours to drive and see this byway.

evidence.claim: Its description emphasizes rocky shores, granite mountains, lakes and spruce-fir forest.
evidence.quote: From craggy shorelines and granite-capped mountains to crystal lakes and spruce–fir forests

evidence.claim: The 27-mile Park Loop Road follows a mostly one-way, clockwise course, with a two-way section returning toward Hulls Cove.
evidence.quote: 27 miles (43 km) long, it traverses the eastern side of Mount Desert Island in a (mostly) one-way, clockwise direction, from Bar Harbor to Seal Harbor. (The road is two-way for a section between Wildwood Stables, toward the middle of Mount Desert Island, and the Hulls Cove entrance near Bar Harbor, to the north.)

evidence.claim: Construction of the Park Loop Road stretched from 1921 to 1958, creating access separate from local streets and the non-motorized carriage roads.
evidence.quote: Constructed between 1921 and 1958, it provides access separate from local roads and non-motorized carriage roads

evidence.claim: John D. Rockefeller Jr. guided the motor road’s completion.
evidence.quote: Completed, under the guidance of John D. Rockefeller Jr., in 1958, after a 37-year process

evidence.claim: He had also developed the carriage-road network after automobiles were allowed throughout the island in 1915, seeking routes isolated from motor traffic.
evidence.quote: Despite their efforts to keep the island free of motor vehicles, their presence was authorized across the whole island by 1915. John D. Rockefeller Jr., who had a large summer house on the southeastern part of the island, in response embarked on a major effort to build a network of carriage roads on its eastern half, which would be isolated from the roads open to motor vehicles

evidence.claim: The carriage bridges used hand-hewn local granite and were designed to fit the landscape, with places to view the scenery and to see the bridges themselves.
evidence.quote: The bridges in the network are all built out of hand-hewn locally quarried granite.  They were specifically designed to blend into the landscape in an organic manner, and are sited so that they may be used as viewing platforms for the scenery, and so that they may themselves be viewed.

evidence.claim: From Trenton, follow Route 3 across Thompson Island and into Bar Harbor before joining the park drive.
evidence.quote: Continuing along route 3, visitors will cross Thompson Island

evidence.quote: Jordan Pond, Pemetic Mountain, the Bubbles, Bubble Rock, Bubble Pond, Eagle Lake, and the side road to the summit of Cadillac Mountain.

evidence.claim: Thunder Hole is a crevasse into which waves crash, on the coastal stretch of the Park Loop Road after Sand Beach.
evidence.quote: Thunder Hole (a crevasse into which waves crash loudly)

evidence.claim: after Sand Beach

evidence.quote: Thunder Hole Gorham Mountain trailhead Boulder Beach Otter Cliff overlook

evidence.claim: This shoreline alternates between rocky headlands and beaches eroded into stones or sand.
evidence.quote: Acadia has a coastline composed of rocky headlands, and more heavily eroded stony or sandy beaches.

evidence.claim: In winter, only the section from the entrance station to Otter Cliff Road usually remains open to vehicles. Check park closure alerts.
evidence.quote: Check alerts for road closures during the winter months. Only one section (from the Entrance Station to Otter Cliff Road) usually remains open to vehicles.

evidence.claim: Ice formed Jordan Pond, and glacial debris helps contain its southern end alongside an artificial dam.
evidence.quote: The pond was formed by the Wisconsin Ice Sheet during the last glacial period.

evidence.claim: glacial debris helps contain its southern end alongside an artificial dam
evidence.quote: The southern end is constrained by glacial debris and an artificial dam.

evidence.claim: Penobscot Mountain rises to the west, Pemetic to the east, and the Bubbles above the northeastern shore.
evidence.quote: Penobscot Mountain (1194 ft) rises to the west, while Pemetic Mountain (1247 ft) rises to the east. Two roche moutonnées known as The Bubbles (North and South) rise above the northeastern shoreline.

evidence.claim: The pond reaches a maximum depth of 150 feet and supplies drinking water to Seal Harbor.
evidence.quote: The pond covers 187 acres (76 ha) to a maximum depth of 150 feet (46 m)

evidence.claim: supplies drinking water to Seal Harbor
evidence.quote: it is the water supply for the village of Seal Harbor.

evidence.claim: At the southern end, the original Jordan Pond House restaurant dated from the 1870s.
evidence.quote: In the 1870s a restaurant known as the Jordan Pond House was built.

evidence.claim: At the southern end
evidence.quote: primarily the tea-house at the southern end

evidence.claim: It burned in June 1979; private fundraising financed a new building.
evidence.quote: The original building was destroyed by fire in June 1979, and a new building was financed through private fund raising.

evidence.claim: A walking trail circles the pond, with branches leading to other park features; a carriage trail follows an adjacent ridge.
evidence.quote: The pond is ringed by a walking trail, from which trails branch off to other park features. One of the park's original carriage trails runs along an adjacent ridge.

evidence.claim: The Bubbles rise above the pond’s northeastern shoreline.
evidence.quote: Two roche moutonnées known as The Bubbles (North and South) rise above the northeastern shoreline.

evidence.claim: Before the summit road, visitors reached the Green Mountain Hotel by cog railway.
evidence.quote: From 1883 until 1893 the Green Mountain Cog Railway ran to the summit to take visitors to the Green Mountain Hotel.

evidence.claim: The hotel burned in 1895, and the train was sold and moved to New Hampshire’s Mount Washington Cog Railway.
evidence.quote: The hotel burned down in 1895 and the cog train was sold and moved to the Mount Washington Cog Railway in New Hampshire.

evidence.claim: Green Mountain became Cadillac Mountain in 1918, taking the name of French explorer Antoine de La Mothe Cadillac.
evidence.quote: Before being renamed in 1918, the mountain had been called Green Mountain. The new name honors the French explorer and adventurer Antoine de La Mothe Cadillac.

evidence.claim: The summit road followed: construction began in 1925 and ended in 1931.
evidence.quote: The Cadillac Mountain Summit Road, begun in 1925, was completed in 1931.

evidence.claim: A paved road and hiking trails now reach the summit.
evidence.quote: There are various hiking trails and a paved road that lead to the summit of Cadillac Mountain.

evidence.claim: Along Cadillac Mountain Road, bodies of black diabase rock record later volcanic activity that intruded into the mountain’s granite.
evidence.quote: A fine-grained, black igneous rock called diabase intruded into the granite during later volcanic activity. Diabase bodies, or dikes, are visible along the Cadillac Mountain road and on the Schoodic Peninsula.

evidence.claim: During the busy season, Cadillac Summit Road requires a vehicle reservation in addition to a park entrance pass.
evidence.quote: In 2021, the park began requiring a vehicle reservation to drive up the Cadillac Summit Road during the busy season, roughly late May to late October, to ease traffic and parking congestion on Cadillac Mountain. The reservations cost $6 per vehicle in addition to a park entrance pass
